decisions.reason: In the Analysis section (p. 1164) and Discussion (p. 1173), Watts, Duncan, and Quan (2018) explicitly group Mischel, Shoda, and Peake (1988), Mischel, Shoda, and Rodriguez (1989), and Shoda, Mischel, and Peake (1990) as the studies they attempted to replicate and extend; thus 1988 is not merely incidental background. However, throughout the Abstract, Introduction, Method, Analysis, Results, and Discussion, every concrete experimental parameter (the diagnostic condition with exposed rewards and no suggested ideation strategies, n = 35-48) and numerical age-15 benchmark (SAT math r = .57, SAT verbal r = .42, parent-reported attention r = .39) is attributed specifically to Shoda et al. (1990), which is already represented by shipped row 484 (DOI 10.1037/0012-1649.26.6.978). The primary text of Watts et al. (2018) never separates a distinct empirical claim tested specifically from Mischel et al. (1988) versus Shoda et al. (1990), and the original 1988 and 1990 primary texts are unavailable in this packet to establish whether the tested adolescent competency associations are fully captured under report equivalence by shipped row 484 or constitute a separate retested finding from 1988.

decisions.location: Results ('Response time varies sub-linearly by lag to the more recent item'), p. 6 (chunk 17), and Introduction, p. 2 (chunk 4)
decisions.quote:
The ﬁnding of sublinearity is visually consistent with prior studies (Hacker, 1980;
Hockley, 1984). However to our knowledge it had not previously been statistically evaluated.
decisions.reason: Singh and Howard (2017) closely follow the rapid consonant-list relative judgment-of-recency (JOR) procedure of Experiment 2 of Hacker (1980), represented by shipped row 90 (DOI 10.1037/0278-7393.6.6.651). For the classic finding that correct RT depends on the lag to the more recent probe and not the less recent probe, Hacker (1980) Experiment 2 is the closest-chain empirical target whose specific experimental protocol and result are replicated. Regarding the sublinear increase of correct RT with lag to the more recent item, both the Introduction (p. 2) and Results (p. 6) state that while sublinearity is visually consistent with the plotted curves in Hacker (1980, Fig. 5) and Hockley (1984, Fig. 7), to the authors' knowledge it had never previously been statistically evaluated, and testing whether the RT increase is linear or sublinear is where the current experiment breaks new ground. Because evaluating sublinearity is a novel statistical extension rather than a retest of a prior statistical finding—and the visual comparison itself is already present in shipped row 90 (Hacker, 1980)—Hockley (1984) is not an omitted retested target.

decisions.location: Introduction, p. 5, lines 148-156 (and Behavioral Experiments, p. 9, lines 287-297; Discussion, pp. 34-36; References, p. 38)
decisions.quote:
The results revealed mainly parallel self-terminating processing in
the OR condition, with participants being able to stop processing as soon as either channel
had completed processing. In contrast, and unlike Cheng et al. (2018), participants in the
AND condition showed some evidence for coactive processing.
      To further investigate the difference in these findings, we extend our investigation
of face processing to schematic faces similar to Fifić and Townsend’s (2010) using the
paradigm developed in Cheng et al. (2018).
decisions.reason: Cheng and Little explicitly design Experiment 2 to investigate the discrepancy between Cheng et al. (2018) (shipped row 2259, DOI 10.1037/xlm0000479, which used morphed faces and found independent serial/parallel processing without coactivity) and Fifić and Townsend (2010) (which used schematic faces manipulated on eye separation and lip position in an SFT categorization task and found some coactive processing as well as exhaustive contrast-category processing / weak holism). Experiment 2 adopts schematic faces with fixed feature-spacing values in the Cheng et al. (2018) categorization paradigm, states an explicit directional prediction for reproducing Fifić and Townsend's (2010) coactivity finding with schematic faces (p. 9, lines 287-297), and directly evaluates its Experiment 2 results (no consistent coactivity and no exhaustive processing) against Fifić and Townsend's (2010) findings in the Results and Discussion (pp. 34-36). Under the codebook, paradigm differences do not exclude a conceptual replication that empirically retests a published finding, and shipped row 2259 does not cover Fifić and Townsend (2010).

decisions.location: References, p. 269, lines 751-752 (and Discussion, pp. 266-268, lines 602-670)
decisions.quote:
Xu, E (1993, March). The concept of object identity. Paper presented at the biennial meeting
     of the Society for Research in Child Development, New Orleans, LA.
decisions.reason: In the Discussion (pp. 266-268), Simon, Hespos, and Rochat (1995) explicitly compare their own impossible-identity condition results in 5-month-old infants to Xu's (1993) two occlusion experiments with 10-month-old infants and conclude that their study replicated both Wynn (1992) (shipped row 2196, DOI 10.1038/358749a0) and Xu (1993) on infants ignoring changes in object identity in favor of spatiotemporal specification. While this is a genuine empirical own-result comparison rather than mere background, the References section (p. 269, lines 751-752) positively identifies Xu (1993) as an unpublished conference presentation ('Paper presented at the biennial meeting of the Society for Research in Child Development, New Orleans, LA'), and no published article for Xu's finding existed prior to this 1995 article (submitted July 1994). Because the codebook requires an earlier published empirical finding and expressly excludes unpublished conference presentations/abstracts, Xu (1993) is not an eligible target.

decisions.location: Abstract (Results), lines 22-23 (chunk 2), and Publisher-deposited reference metadata (bb0065, bb0105, bb0110)
decisions.quote: CFA confirmed the underlying domain structure to be same as for the FSFI, supporting the factorial validity of the modified questionnaire. In addition, successful replication of the psychometric properties of the original FSFI was demonstrated.
decisions.reason: The available primary source for Burri, Cherkas, and Spector (2010) consists only of the abstract and the publisher-deposited Crossref bibliography; the main text, Methods, Results, and tables remain unavailable. The abstract reports that CFA confirmed the underlying domain structure of the FSFI and that 'successful replication of the psychometric properties of the original FSFI was demonstrated,' without naming specific authors or publication years. Although the deposited reference list includes the foundational 19-item, 6-domain FSFI development paper by Rosen et al. (2000) (bb0065, DOI 10.1080/009262300278597, shipped row 666), it also includes separate empirical FSFI psychometric validation studies in distinct cohorts—specifically Meston (2003, bb0105, DOI 10.1080/713847100) and Wiegel, Meston, and Rosen (2005, bb0110, DOI 10.1080/00926230590475206), as well as Sand et al. (2009), Chang et al. (2009), and Isidori et al. (2010). Without the full text, it is impossible to verify whether the psychometric replication in Burri et al. (2010) is restricted to shipped row 666 (Rosen et al., 2000) or also empirically retests specific validation benchmarks from Meston (2003) or Wiegel et al. (2005).

decisions.location: Introduction, p. 368, lines 56-60 (and Section I / I.A, pp. 371-375, Figure 2; References, p. 404)
decisions.quote:
In reality, demand for
income redistribution in the United States has remained ﬂat by some mea-
sures and decreased according to others (see Kuziemko and others 2013),
as we document later in this paper.
decisions.reason: Ashok, Kuziemko, and Washington (2015) cite Kuziemko et al. (2013, NBER WP 18865; explicitly linked in References, p. 404, to its revised published 2015 American Economic Review article) for the finding that U.S. demand for redistribution has remained flat or decreased since the 1970s (p. 368) and re-estimate this trend in Section I / I.A (pp. 371-375, Figure 2). Primary inspection of Kuziemko et al. (2013) confirms that Figure 1 (p. 33; discussed on p. 1) empirically plots and fits the historical U.S. General Social Survey (GSS) eqwlth series since 1978, separate from its mTurk randomized experiments. In Section I.A, Ashok et al. re-analyze the same pre-2013 historical GSS eqwlth observations (1978-2006 focal trend and full series through 2012, adding no post-2012 GSS waves) using their own sample exclusions (spanint != 2), weights (wtssall * oversamp), and partisan-unit scaling to ensure heterogeneous patterns are not driven by data or coding differences, and check robustness across two other historical GSS questions (helppoor, helpnot, 1975-2006/2012) and ANES (1972-2008). Because this re-analyzes the same historical survey series for coding/measure robustness rather than new data waves, it is a valid omitted reproduction target distinct from shipped row 2155 (Kenworthy & McCall, 2007/2008).
